target: AG1’s claim that AI makes work faster and more effective, benefits the economy, and can be deployed responsibly with accessibility and safety benefits.
objection: Faster AI-assisted work may actually mean fewer jobs, lower wages, and more profit concentration among the firms that own the models, harming workers and small businesses rather than simply adding convenience.

target: AG1’s claim that AI is a practical accessibility tool.
objection: Accessibility tools often come with privacy tradeoffs because they may require microphones, text, browsing, or behavioral inference, which can expose users to surveillance or misuse.

target: AG1’s claim that AI improves health and workplace safety.
objection: AI systems can be biased or error-prone, so when they are trained on biased data or tested unevenly they can misdiagnose or misjudge risk, worsening outcomes for marginalized groups instead of improving safety or health.

target: AG1’s claim that AI helps students and professionals and that its harms can be managed with responsible use.
objection: AI can undermine critical thinking because people who rely on it for writing, studying, and decision-making practice less reasoning, which weakens educational outcomes for both students and adults.

target: AG1’s reliance on the phrase ‘when designed and used responsibly’ as a safeguard.
objection: That assumption is too weak because real-world incentives favor deployment and monetization over preventing privacy violations, bias, and labor displacement.

target: AG2’s claim that AI is bad because companies will reduce jobs or wages and workers will be displaced.
objection: Job loss or wage suppression is not inevitable: AI often augments work rather than replacing entire roles, and societies can use reskilling and transition programs while AI also creates new kinds of work.

target: AG2’s claim that AI assistive tools inevitably create privacy harms.
objection: Privacy tradeoffs are not inherent to accessibility tools; systems can use on-device processing, meaningful consent, data minimization, transparency, and audits, so privacy risks are solvable by design and policy.

target: AG2’s claim that AI cannot reliably improve health or safety because it may be biased or inaccurate.
objection: Biased or error-prone systems are a reason for strong evaluation and human oversight, not a reason to reject AI entirely; with safeguards, AI can improve triage and detect hazards earlier than humans alone.

target: AG2’s claim that AI undermines critical thinking and therefore should be treated as broadly harmful.
objection: AI can also be used as a tutor or feedback tool that explains concepts, gives practice problems, and checks understanding, so the issue is how it is used rather than the existence of AI itself.

target: AG2’s claim that market incentives make responsible use unrealistic.
objection: That is an argument for regulation and governance, not for concluding that AI itself is bad; audits, privacy standards, accountability, and rules for high-risk uses can address the incentive problem.

target: AG1’s general claim that AI benefits society if risks are ‘manageable’ through governance.
objection: Saying risks are manageable is not enough because enforcement is weak in practice: regulators are under-resourced, standards get diluted, and companies move faster than oversight can keep up, so partial compliance is the realistic outcome.

target: AG1’s claim that job transitions and reskilling neutralize AI’s economic harms.
objection: Reskilling does not erase the displacement costs, lower bargaining power, and wage pressure AI can create for workers and small businesses; augmentation can still mean fewer hires and more precarity.

target: AG1’s claim that human-in-the-loop safeguards can fix high-stakes AI failures.
objection: Human review does not guarantee correctness when model outputs are biased, the reviewer is pressured by speed or cost, or the system’s objective is misaligned with welfare; harms can merely change form instead of disappearing.

target: AG1’s claim that AI can be used as a tutor without harming cognition.
objection: Tutoring tools can make it easier to offload thinking through drafts, answers, and translations, which undermines assessment validity and reduces genuine practice; this is built into the product incentives, not just a usage policy issue.

target: AG1’s claim that AI’s harms can be handled by governance rather than opposing the technology.
objection: The incentives and scaling dynamics are structurally misaligned with responsible deployment, so society should not assume governance will reliably contain the harms.

target: AG1’s claim that AI is beneficial because benefits outweigh risks if we govern it responsibly.
objection: AG1 has not shown that the benefits reliably outweigh widespread harms in practice; the burden is on the pro-AI side to prove a net positive, not merely to say it is possible.

target: AG1’s claim that AI does not uniquely amplify inequality because humans are also biased.
objection: AI trained on historical data and deployed at scale can repeat and amplify unequal outcomes in hiring, credit, policing, and eligibility decisions, making racial harms routine rather than occasional.

target: AG1’s comparison of AI governance to medicine and other regulated technologies.
objection: That comparison is weak because medicine is tightly bounded and accountable, while AI is broadly deployed, iteratively updated, and embedded into many decision points, making oversight much harder.

target: AG1’s claim that bias can be handled by auditing and evaluation.
objection: Audits often measure only what is easy to measure and may not reflect what people actually experience; teams can optimize metrics while downstream disparities remain, so audits do not eliminate bias.

target: AG1’s claim that continuous governance tools like model cards, regression tests, and incident reporting can keep AI accountable.
objection: Those governance tools are undermined by proprietary opacity and rapid model updates, which prevent external communities and researchers from verifying harms in real time.

target: AG1’s claim that AI is acceptable because humans also have bias.
objection: Human bias is not a defense because AI automates decisions at scale and speed, increasing the volume, consistency, and reach of biased outcomes.

target: AG1’s claim that concentration can be fixed with antitrust, interoperability, and portability rules.
objection: Dominant AI firms can still preserve power through massive compute costs, proprietary data pipelines, talent advantages, and closed APIs, so concentration harms will not reliably disappear just because regulation tries to address them.

target: AG1’s claim that training-data privacy can be fixed with licensed datasets, minimization, and privacy-preserving techniques.
objection: Training privacy is not fixable so easily because foundation models usually rely on large-scale scraping and data collection that is not meaningfully consented to by the people whose data is included, and the resulting model may absorb sensitive patterns that cannot be cleanly controlled later.

target: AG1’s claim that general-purpose AI can be safely limited to beneficial use cases.
objection: When general AI capability is widely available, spillover into surveillance, automated decisions, cheating, and other higher-risk uses is hard to stop because the same underlying systems can be repurposed quickly.

target: AG1’s claim that broad opposition is worse because it blocks good uses and pushes development into less transparent channels.
objection: Even if some good uses exist, the underlying mechanisms of market concentration, data-driven training, and general-purpose spillover make the promised safeguards unreliable in practice, so society should prioritize alternatives that do not depend on pervasive data extraction and automated judgment at scale.

target: AG1’s claim that monitoring and licensing can be privacy-preserving and therefore solve oversight problems.
objection: Meaningful monitoring and enforcement often require visibility into systems and user interactions, which expands data collection and creates more privacy risk rather than eliminating it.

target: AG1’s claim that harmful effects can be rolled back or prevented before they matter.
objection: Many harms are effectively irreversible once training data have been captured or a biased system has been deployed, because the damage to people and systems remains even after the model is changed or withdrawn.

target: AG1’s claim that capability-based or use-case-based regulation can keep general-purpose AI safe.
objection: General-purpose models are repurposed so quickly that clean use-case boundaries break down, and regulators cannot keep up with constant changes in model behavior and deployment context.

target: AG1’s claim that privacy-preserving governance can protect users during AI use.
objection: The bigger privacy problem happens earlier, during dataset collection and model training, where scraping, brokerage, and unclear consent already compromise privacy before any monitoring of usage begins.

target: AG1’s claim that rollback and prevention make harms manageable.
objection: Rollback is not a real undo button because harmful outputs, discriminatory decisions, leaked sensitive information, and downstream copies can have immediate and lasting effects even if a release is later withdrawn.

target: AG1’s claim that capability-based rules can stay ahead of model evolution.
objection: Capability-based regulation assumes stable and legible behavior, but models are updated, fine-tuned, and embedded in tools that change how they work, so regulators can be perpetually behind.

target: AG1’s claim that dataset provenance, privacy-by-design, and stronger pre-deployment controls can make AI safe enough.
objection: Dataset provenance is often not practically verifiable, privacy-by-design cannot eliminate inference and reconstruction harms, and pre-deployment controls cannot stop downstream harms from third-party use or persistent copies of models.

target: AG1’s claim that audits and disclosure can make AI safer without blanket opposition.
objection: Even imperfect oversight still leaves recurring harms, and those harms are borne disproportionately by individuals and marginalized groups while most benefits accrue to companies and early adopters.

target: AG1’s claim that educational AI harms can be managed with process-based assessments and AI tutoring that checks understanding.
objection: Students still face strong incentives to use AI to generate plausible work quickly, which creates an arms race for teachers and can turn assessment into a verification burden rather than genuine learning.

target: AG1’s claim that AI tutoring can strengthen study habits and thinking.
objection: An AI tutor can provide correct-looking answers and explanations even when the student’s reasoning is flawed, so students may learn to trust outputs instead of building internal skills.

target: AG1’s claim that accountability in education can be achieved with transparency rules and audits without major privacy costs.
objection: Educational enforcement often requires monitoring student interactions to detect misuse and discrimination, which increases privacy risk and creates the same surveillance tradeoff the pro-AI side is trying to avoid.

target: AG1’s claim that schools can solve the AI problem with redesigned assessments and non-invasive checks.
objection: Process-based assessments, oral defenses, and verification tasks require time, staff, and smaller classes, so they are much less deployable in under-resourced schools and can widen educational inequality.

target: AG1’s claim that students can only use AI appropriately if schools design good verification tasks.
objection: Even with verification prompts, students can outsource the verification itself to AI, creating a circular loop in which the apparent reasoning may also be AI-generated.

target: AG1’s claim that data minimization and random checks can preserve privacy in AI-enabled education.
objection: Even supposedly minimal enforcement still involves storing submissions, logs, and interaction artifacts, and those records often expand over time, increasing privacy exposure.

target: AG1’s claim that AI can be deployed equitably in schools through vetted tools, training, and guardrails.
objection: Under-resourced schools are least likely to implement those safeguards well, so AI’s cognitive and fairness harms concentrate where students already have the least ability to compensate.

target: AG1’s claim that redesigned assessments and verification tasks can stop outsourcing.
objection: Students can still use AI in real time for planning, drafting, and checking explanations, which turns the classroom into a constant arms race and still fails to measure genuine understanding reliably.

target: AG1’s claim that data-minimizing accountability avoids privacy costs.
objection: Even minimized logs and audits can accumulate into detailed educational profiles over time, and institutions often expand retention later for legal or disciplinary reasons, so the privacy tradeoff remains.

target: AG1’s claim that classroom capability restrictions and procurement rules can keep AI limited to safe educational uses.
objection: General-purpose models can be repurposed through prompting, workflows, and tool chaining, so a supposed distinction between ‘assistive’ and ‘generative’ use is not a stable boundary in practice.

target: AG1’s claim that procurement standards and funding can prevent vendor drift and keep schools safe.
objection: Vendors can still update products iteratively in ways that increase data collection or add proctoring-like features, so continuous enforcement would be needed and schools often lack the capacity for that.

target: AG1’s claim that retention limits and audited exceptions can stop privacy creep.
objection: Retention limits are routinely weakened by claims about safety, quality, or legal defense, so privacy restrictions become a moving target rather than a dependable safeguard.

target: AG1’s claim that technical gating can stop misuse of classroom AI.
objection: Even if a tool cannot generate a full submission, students can still outsource thinking by asking for hints, planning, and reasoning checks, so the critical-thinking harm remains.

target: AG1’s claim that classroom boundaries can be enforced through technical controls and teacher-approved templates.
objection: General-purpose systems are flexible and can be bypassed through prompting strategies, alternative interfaces, exporting text, or peer sharing, so the boundary is not stable in practice.

target: AG1’s claim that procurement change-control and service-level agreements can stop vendor drift.
objection: Vendors can still ship updates that alter telemetry, logging, personalization, or integrations, and most districts cannot continuously monitor or enforce those changes well enough to keep up.

target: AG1’s claim that hard retention caps and audited exceptions solve privacy creep.
objection: Any system that allows logs for investigation, audit, or dispute resolution still creates a privacy-cost tradeoff, while reducing retention can also weaken accountability, so the problem is not eliminated.
